name: Handshake styles

lead: A handshake is one of the first physical signals in a meeting, and guides in looksmaxxing communities treat it as a way to come across as confident. The style elements discussed are grip firmness, how the palms meet, the angle of the arm, and eye contact.

Practised handshake form is cited as helping in interviews and social settings. Cultural sources add that expectations differ: a firm grip is traditional in the US, UK and Canada, while softer grips are customary in parts of the Middle East and Asia.

paras: Guides describe a firm but not crushing grip, palm-to-palm contact with the webbing between thumb and index finger meeting the other person's, one or two pumps, and eye contact. One thread suggests holding a drink in the left hand so the right is free.
Handshakes can transfer microbes, and some people avoid them for religious or health reasons. Forcing a very hard grip can be uncomfortable for the other person, and customs differ across cultures.

chain: Firm, well-placed grip with eye contact
angle.text: The handshake is one of the first moments of contact, so guides present grip and eye contact as shaping how confident someone seems. The value is social presence rather than a change in physical features.

lead: Handshake styles are the variations in how people shake hands: grip strength, hand placement, arm angle, duration and eye contact. Looksmaxxing guides present a well-formed handshake as a cheap upgrade to first impressions, advantageous in job interviews and social events [1].

The handshake is old: a ninth-century BC Assyrian relief shows King Shalmaneser III clasping the hand of a Babylonian king to seal an alliance, and the Greeks practised it as dexiosis by the fifth century BC [2]. A traditional handshake in the US, UK and Canada is firm, uses the right hand and comes with good posture and eye contact [2].
Variants include the hand hug, in which the free hand covers the clasped hands, which politicians use to seem warm, and the fist bump, which is less formal [2].
infobox: Grip, palm contact, arm angle, eye contact, pumps

paras: Handshakes convey trust, respect and equality, and mark greetings, partings, congratulations and completed agreements [2]. Style choices include a firm traditional grip, the hand hug, the fist bump, and the snap handshake customary in Liberia [2].

A looksmax.org guide lists four elements: a firm grip, hand positioning so the webbing between thumb and index finger touches the other person's, the arm entry angle, and eye contact [1]. It says too hard is better than too soft and that gripping only fingertips looks timid [1]. Some of its framing about status and dominance reflects the poster's views rather than etiquette consensus. A T Nation thread, Limp Handshakes, shows a related view in lifting communities that older business contacts respond to a firm handshake with eye contact [3].

Grips are softer in the Middle East and Turkey, in China elders are greeted first with a weak grip, Japan favours bowing, and Indonesia advises a medium-to-soft grip [2]. In India namaste is common and in Thailand the wai [2].
Handshakes can spread microbes, and a 2014 study cited by Wikipedia found fist bumps and high fives spread fewer germs [2]. During COVID-19, elbow bumps and namaste were promoted as alternatives [2].
